summary: MarsTrek is a suit-tablet Marswalk planner that answers the question every future Mars crew will face: can we walk there and still get home safely? As missions move from landing to exploring on foot, a wrong turn costs time, resources and safety, and a map alone cannot tell a crew whether a walk is survivable. Built on real NASA and USGS data, MarsTrek turns the terrain of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater into a plan for the whole walk, out and back. A crew picks a habitat and a destination, compares candidate routes by slope, time and climb, adjusts the suit and load, then follows a live trip with a turn-back point and a return check, while oxygen, battery, coolant and CO2 scrubber are tracked and radiation dose is estimated. For the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, we turn a map into a survival decision, giving planners, trainers and crews a low-cost way to rehearse walks before anyone leaves the habitat. Today MarsTrek is a working prototype with adjustable assumptions, and our roadmap includes boulder mapping, real suit data and emergency backup.
details:
What it does and how it works


MARS Treck is a browser-based Marswalk planner for a suit tablet, set on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. A crew picks a habitat and a destination. The app computes candidate routes over real terrain slope, compares them by distance, trip time, steepest slope, climb and share of slow ground, and lets the crew adjust suit settings and load. A planning engine estimates time, oxygen, battery, coolant, CO2 scrubber and radiation dose for the round trip. A live trip simulation shows arrival time, distance left and a “turn back here” point, and a return check shows whether the way home still works at any moment. Science targets come with real Curiosity photos and saved notes.

Key technical innovations

  • Return-first planning. The way home is part of the plan from the start, not an afterthought. Most Mars maps only show where things are.
  • A live turn-back point and return check. The app turns a map into a survival decision that can be re-evaluated at any moment during the walk.
  • Terrain-based route comparison. Routes are scored on distance, time, steepest slope, climb and share of slow ground, all derived from real elevation data.
  • Full life-support accounting. Oxygen, battery, coolant, CO2 scrubber and radiation dose are tracked together across the round trip.
  • A walking-effort model scaled to Mars gravity. This turns slope into realistic effort and time. Your references cite Minetti et al. 2002 for walking energy cost at extreme slopes.
  • Imaginary habitats. Crews can compare the best way home from several possible habitat locations.
  • Adjustable suit assumptions. The suit and load are editable, so planners can test different scenarios.
  • A safety-first data rule. Ground with missing elevation data is treated as no-go.
  • Honest limits built in. The 20 m slope map cannot see boulders, the radiation figure is a surface baseline and not a suit dose, and only CTX is sharp enough for walking decisions.
  • A modern, light stack. React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet and Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel with code on GitHub, so it needs no installation.
  • Data from real sources. The project uses 85 Curiosity rover positions, boxwork mapping (Siebach and Grotzinger 2014) and raw Curiosity images.

Benefits and intended impact
Crews, mission planners and trainers can rehearse a walk, and its way home, before anyone leaves the habitat. The intended impact is better turnaround decisions on future Mars missions, and a low-cost training tool that turns open NASA data into a survival decision.

Business model Integration

MarsTrek helps Mars crews decide when to go on and when to turn back by planning the whole walk, out and back, before anyone leaves the habitat. Built on open NASA and USGS data, it runs in any browser, so it is low-cost to try. We propose licences for planning and training teams, terrain data subscriptions, custom builds and research grants, all still to be validated. Today it is a working prototype.

Cost Volume table

Data Sets


NASA/JPL Mars Trek map tiles (CTX, MOLA, THEMIS), the USGS Gale merged elevation model (resampled from 1 m to 20 m and converted to slope), Curiosity RAD radiation (about 0.67 mSv per day), 85 Curiosity rover positions, boxwork mapping (Siebach and Grotzinger 2014), and raw Curiosity images.

Tools
React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet and Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel with code on GitHub. Slope maps were made from the elevation data with image processing. We used AI assistants (Claude and Codex) for planning, coding and presentation help. [Edit to match what your team really used.] No special hardware is needed: it runs in any browser.

Use of AI Tools:

  • ChatGPT – Research assistance, technical guidance, problem solving, and documentation.
  • Claude – Code generation, code review, debugging, and improving project implementation.

Presenting Data and Results

Creativity
Most Mars maps show where things are. We plan the whole walk, out and back, and treat the way home as part of the plan from the start. We also add imaginary habitats to compare the best way home, a walking-effort model scaled to Mars gravity, and adjustable suit assumptions, all in one view.

Factors we considered

  • Safety first: ground with missing elevation data is treated as no-go.
  • Honest limits: 20 m slope can’t see boulders, radiation is a surface baseline and not a suit dose, and suit numbers are adjustable assumptions, not NASA specifications.
  • Data quality: only CTX is sharp enough for walking decisions, so the other layers are regional context.
  • Next steps: boulder mapping from HiRISE, real EVA life-support figures, finer terrain near targets, and an emergency backup that alerts the nearest habitat.
